#9409. What Chimps Can Teach Us About Male Friendships

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Across the Western world, young men and boys face a changing economy, with fewer manual labor jobs and factory floors that used to give a swathe of working-class men purpose and value. This leaves a large portion of recent generations feeling left behind and forgotten—and vulnerable to exploitation.

A profitable industry of influencers who misframe evolutionary science to justify their narratives have taken advantage of the addictive nature of social media to hook into this vacuum and light up phone screens every night with the same vitriolic messages: “Reclaim your manhood”; “You are being feminized”; “The world is making you soft.”

But this narrative conflicts with the biological reality. Across species—from fungal networks trading nutrients underground to astronauts sharing the role of emptying the latrine on the International Space Station—every organism must strike some balance between competing and cooperating. Lessons from the animal kingdom, from my research and others, show that cooperation doesn’t diminish masculinity.

Indeed, dominant primates use their power judiciously, and male friendship forms the foundation of cooperation in a variety of species, with affectionate touch, caring, and vulnerability playing crucial roles in male relationships. The simple picture painted for these boys is built on sand. Once we observe the reality of sex, behavior, and connection in the natural world around us, it washes away.

Human males stand to improve their relationships, benefit from a broader base of emotional and social support, and enhance their well-being with these friendship lessons from our closest cousins in the animal kingdom.

One term at the core of the manosphere is the notion of alpha males. Life coaches and politicians push this construct without understanding the true function of hierarchy in the natural world. They believe that to get ahead you must take advantage of others, and that the weak get left behind. In reality, dominant male primates care for relationships and wield their power judiciously.

It’s true that male chimpanzees form typically linear dominance relationships, where one submits to another, all the way to the top. They compete, and those competitions can spill into physical altercations. Higher-ranking males do tend to sire more offspring.

But these broad truths hide the nuance of layered cooperation, care, nurturing touch, and love among male chimps. Day after day, most of that competitive pressure never turns into a fight at all. What holds chimpanzee communities together is less the male at the top and more the alliances underneath him. Males groom each other for hours at a time. They embrace after conflicts and kiss the arms and shoulders of their allies before potential competition, to resolve any tension. Before risky boundary patrols, when they might encounter rival groups, they even hold each other’s genitals—a sign of deep trust. Data spanning nearly three decades from Gombe show that males with strong ties to the alpha sired more offspring than those without, and so did males with wider networks of close allies, whether or not they ever rose in rank at all. Those who look out for each other and contribute to a strong community end up thriving.

You can see the value of those alliances when a hierarchy is disrupted. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, Anna Preis and her colleagues measured urinary cortisol in wild males across stable and unstable dominance periods. Stress rose in every male during the unstable stretches, regardless of rank. Aggression went the other way, rising when things were calm and the group faced less risk of destabilization. When the risk of escalation was greatest, males backed off. Stability has its own payoff; a group tearing itself apart can’t defend a territory.

Indeed, even in its origins, the term “alpha” contained more nuance than broadly understood. The term rose out of research during the mid-20th century on captive wolves who were thrown together into crowded spaces without room to escape. Such an arrangement would produce a tense, despotic dynamic in any species, including our own. Once biologists began studying wild wolf packs, it became apparent that they are, well, families. They comprise a breeding pair and their grown offspring. L. David Mech, the biologist who popularized the alpha wolf in the first place, has spent more than two decades asking people to retire the term in order to accurately reflect natural communities. Despite its inaccuracy, the idea still perpetuates on podcasts and social media.

The role of vulnerability and comfort in the natural world provides another powerful lesson for humanity. At a wildlife sanctuary in Zambia, I’ve come to know a longstanding alpha male chimpanzee named Doug over many years. One day, during my first field season observing his group, he was separated from his community for routine husbandry purposes, alongside a slightly younger rival and the rival’s paternal ally. During this separation, the rival pair ambushed him, leaving him incredibly shaken. I had known Doug as a strong leader who never broke composure, and I felt shocked to see him cowering and screaming, nothing like the composed figurehead his group had respected.

A low-ranking male, whom Doug had rarely paid attention to, approached first, offering himself in a gesture of submission. What followed drew in most of the roughly 40 other chimpanzees in the group. They embraced, touched, and kissed him; exchanged genital contact; placed their hands in his mouth; and invited him to mount them. This scale of collective reassurance directed toward a single individual is something I’ve never seen since, and is likely only sparked by moments of genuine crisis. The whole group responded to Doug’s distress with an outpouring of comfort and what to humans would appear to be love.

The main aim of this project was to study consolation: how chimpanzees, and their sister species bonobos, comfort each other after fights. But we kept noticing similar intense, friendly contacts occurring in the absence of conflicts, often in the anticipation of competition. To better understand this, we conducted a feeding task with a five-minute window before the food arrived, filming 116 apes across five groups at two sanctuaries. We found that those who exchanged more reassuring contact beforehand went on to spend significantly more time feeding peacefully alongside others. In chimpanzees, males exhibited most of this behavior, but primarily in Doug’s more tolerant group. In a more despotic group where resources were less evenly distributed, the male-male relationships were markedly weaker. Simply put, friendship and reassuring behaviors among males helped these chimps peacefully put aside competing interests, which may lay the groundwork for collective harmony.

Some of these behaviors require remarkable trust. Placing a finger, or even a whole hand, inside another male’s mouth or pressing your own mouth to someone’s body after they’ve just been attacked may be misinterpreted as having aggressive intent and could spark a new conflict. Chimpanzees have a reputation for amputating the extremities of others, and that, along with the size of their canines, makes these behaviors exceptionally risky during such turbulent times. Our hypothesis: That could be the point. You only offer that kind of vulnerability to someone you trust not to use it against you, and doing so signals something about the relationship that a show of strength can’t. Again, we noticed that these behaviors were particularly amplified in Doug’s group compared to the one with a less benevolent leader.

Doug remains alpha to this day, and from our research, his tenureship seems to be thanks to the bonds he continues to invest in and the support he shows for his peers. He’s flawed and sometimes lashes out as any male chimpanzee might do, but throughout the seven years we’ve studied him, no challenges have managed to displace him. Doug looks out for others, and in turn they look out for him. Over my time studying many groups of chimpanzees, it seems the most tolerant social environments emerge from the leadership of strong, stable, and generally fair alphas who allow others access to resources and who keep tight bonds with their closest allies.

Humans can also learn from the way male chimpanzees can be tender in other contexts. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, researchers recorded wild chimpanzees adopting orphaned infants, more than half of them taken in by males with no obvious kinship reason to bother. One adult male, Porthos, adopted an unrelated infant female named Gia and carried her on his back for years, sharing food with her long after any potential social debt to her deceased mother had lapsed. Later analysis found that what predicted whether a male took on that role was not the infant’s sex, and not relatedness, but the strength of the grooming bond he’d shared with the mother before she died.

Touch carries power in humans, as well. Research across five European cultures found that the area of the body you’ll let someone touch maps almost directly onto the strength of your emotional bond with them. There is cultural variation. British people are notably more guarded about casual contact than many of their European neighbours, and touch between men in many Western contexts carries particular social weight. Touch conveys intimacy and trust. Yet holding someone’s hand or shoulder can also be used to intimidate or harass. We could learn from primates to stop withholding touch where it would help most and back down from reaching for it where it shouldn’t be used at all.

One key area where more touch helps is sports. A study of all 30 NBA teams during the 2008–09 season found that the teams who touched more early in the season, through fist bumps, chest bumps, hugs, and high fives, went on to perform better and play more cooperatively later, even after controlling for player salaries and pre-season expectations. In women’s college basketball, players who received more physical contact from teammates after missing their first free throw were more likely to convert the second. After five straight shootout losses, England’s governing body in football, the FA, spent 18 months rebuilding England’s approach to penalties under Gareth Southgate, not just the technical side. Players were coached on how to treat each other after a miss. They learned to place an arm around the shoulder rather than leaving each other isolated. Celebrating wildly after a scored kick became a deliberate technique for steadying whoever was up next. Locker-room culture has never been shy about physical contact between teammates. Now we know that the contact might be doing real work.

To be sure, humans show exceptional diversity in our cultures and behavior, for better and worse. But when humans are violent or cruel, people call it primal, or animalistic. We emphasize our altruism as unique to our species. That’s unfair to animals. Humans have bullied others until they took their own lives. We’ve wiped out entire tribes and cultures. And beyond targeting other people, even now, humans are removing protections for endangered keystone species that ecosystems depend upon to thrive. But we don’t need to accept the drive to dominate as inevitable. If the apes show anything, it’s how much of that drive gets managed and set aside day to day, and how much depends on the community you find yourself in. We are a part of the natural world like all other animals, needing to balance our cooperative and competitive urges. And the evidence suggests we sit at the better end of that range far more often than we might think.

Now that we know how central touch and cooperation are to primates and human nature, I hope we can stop being pessimistic when we predict others’ behavior and motives. A study published in Science this June, covering 125 countries and over 100,000 people, found that 69% of us cooperate with a stranger when given the choice. Asked to guess, people put it at 47%. That pessimism showed up in 124 of the 125 countries surveyed. This matters in the grander scheme of things because those of us who expect others to cooperate are far more likely to cooperate also. When researchers simply told participants that most people worldwide see climate change as a threat, belief in others’ willingness to cooperate ticked up, and actual cooperation followed it, slightly, but in the right direction.

Building on the lessons of primate relationships is easier than it seems.

Seek simple interactions. One of the main ways our primate cousins build affiliative relationships is spending time sitting in close proximity. They may groom, or play, or even sit in contact. More often than not they just like to hang out near their close partners. Just being close to one another is meaningful.

Try a car journey or a five-a-side game. Build trust and relationship through activities where nobody has to look anyone in the eye. If a mate isn’t much of a talker, doing something alongside him might get further than sitting him down and asking how he’s doing.

Reach out before a crisis, not after. Great apes exchange most of their reassurance in the tense minutes before competition, not the wreckage afterward. Reconciliation and comforting are commonplace in humans and primates, but it’s much easier to prevent escalation than it is to smooth things over after a fight.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Don’t wait to be the one who’s approached. That 22-point gap between how we actually cooperate and what we think everyone else will do shows the power of offering an invitation to relationship. Most of us are waiting for someone else to go first.

Influencers selling young men and boys on their primal nature fly in the face of the science and what nature actually looks like. Force and competition are real parts of biology, and something we humans have to manage in our everyday lives. But, if there’s one thing I’ve learned from my many years studying our closest relatives, it’s that touch, care, cooperation, and even love are the most instinctive natural components of being part of the primate family.

#9407. MCA Chicago receives gift of 65 works, most of them by women and artists of colour

Gary Simmons’s High Post (2013) Photo: Jim Prinz, courtesy MCA Chicago

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

For Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

The Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and currently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago

The current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn says, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she says. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”

Government funding for the Sydney institution, which is already closed one day a week and is now charging A$20 entry, remains the same as in 2008

This ups the museums holdings of the artist to 22

The gifted works are predominantly by woman-identifying and Bipoc artists, including pieces by Huma Bhabha, Arthur Jafa, Adrian Piper, Jennie C. Jones and Cindy Sherman

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the United States. That is about 17% of all US households — roughly 1 in 6. And the number is growing: the US added over 2 million new millionaire households between 2019 and 2022 alone, even through a global pandemic.

But here is what might surprise you: most millionaires do not look like what you expect. They are not driving Ferraris or living in mansions. The research — most notably from Thomas Stanley and William Danko's landmark study "The Millionaire Next Door" and Chris Hogan's follow-up study of over 10,000 millionaires — consistently shows that the typical American millionaire is a middle-aged person with a modest lifestyle who has been saving and investing for 25-30 years.

This matters for the FI community because it proves that building a million-dollar net worth is not about luck, inheritance, or extraordinary income. It is about consistent behavior applied over time. And if you are on the FI path, you are following the exact same playbook that created 22 million millionaires.

The exact number depends on how you measure it and which data source you use:

The discrepancy between 22 million and 14-15 million comes down to whether you include home equity. If you count total net worth (including home equity), approximately 22 million households qualify. If you count only investable assets (excluding the primary residence), the number drops to about 14-15 million.

For FI purposes, investable assets are the more meaningful measure — your home equity does not fund your retirement spending unless you sell or downsize. But by either measure, the US has more millionaires than any other country in the world.

Note: Growth includes both new wealth creation and inflation. A million dollars in 2000 had the purchasing power of approximately $1.8 million in 2024 dollars.

Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (the largest ever conducted) surveyed over 10,000 millionaires and found: 79% received zero inheritance. The top occupations were engineer, accountant, teacher, management, and attorney — not entrepreneurs or celebrities. 96% said anyone can become a millionaire with discipline and consistent investing. The average millionaire started investing at age 29 and became a millionaire at 49. They are your neighbors, not the people on magazine covers.

The research paints a consistent picture of the typical American millionaire — and it looks very different from what pop culture suggests.

Sources: Chris Hogan National Study of Millionaires, Thomas Stanley "The Millionaire Next Door", Federal Reserve SCF

The path to millionaire status in America overwhelmingly follows a formula, not a lottery ticket:

Millionaires are not "the 1%" — they are the top 10-15%. Here is how wealth is distributed across US households:

Source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, 2022

This means approximately 16% of American households have a net worth of $1 million or more. And the pathway from $500K-$1M (where 11% of households sit) to the millionaire club is often just a matter of continuing to do what they are already doing for another 5-10 years.

The answer depends entirely on two variables: how much you invest each month and what rate of return you earn. Using a conservative 7% average annual real return (the stock market's historical average adjusted for inflation):

Assumes 7% average annual real return with monthly compounding. Results are in today's dollars.

The most striking column is "Growth" — at every savings level, compound growth does a significant portion of the work. An investor saving $1,000/month reaches $1 million in 26 years, but $688,000 of that is investment growth, not contributions. That is the power of compound interest working over decades in low-cost index funds.

FI community members reach millionaire status faster than the average American millionaire (age 49) for three reasons:

A household earning $100,000 with a 50% savings rate ($50,000/year invested) will reach $1 million in approximately 13-14 years at 7% real returns. That is financial independence by age 40-45 if they start at 28-30. This is not theoretical — thousands of FI community members have documented this exact trajectory.

If you are pursuing financial independence, you are on the millionaire path by design. Here is why:

The standard FI formula is 25x your annual spending. If your household spends $40,000 per year, your FI number is $1,000,000 — you are literally targeting millionaire status. If you spend $60,000, your number is $1.5 million. If you spend $80,000, it is $2 million.

Every FI practitioner is building toward a net worth that exceeds $1 million. The difference between the FI community and the general millionaire population is intentionality: FI community members know their number, track their progress monthly, and optimize their savings rate to get there as quickly as possible.

The data from "The Millionaire Next Door" and subsequent research validates the FI approach completely: live below your means, invest the difference in diversified low-cost funds, avoid debt, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting over 15-25 years. That is the millionaire formula. It is also the FI formula. They are the same thing.

The data says this works. 22 million households have already proven it.

Multiply your annual spending by 25. That is your target net worth. For most FI-minded households, this will be $1-2.5 million — squarely in millionaire territory.

Pro tip: Use your ACTUAL spending, not your income. Spending $50,000/year means you need $1.25 million, regardless of whether you earn $60K or $200K.

The average millionaire lived on 75% of their income during accumulation years. FI community members target 30-60%. Every percentage point increase in savings rate accelerates your timeline.

Set up automatic monthly investments into a total stock market index fund. Max out your 401(k) match first, then Roth IRA, then taxable brokerage. Do not try to pick stocks — even professional fund managers fail at this 90% of the time.

73% of millionaires have never carried a credit card balance. Pay off any existing high-interest debt aggressively, then commit to paying your credit card in full every month. Consumer debt is the single biggest destroyer of wealth-building momentum.

Every millionaire tracked their progress. Calculate your net worth on the first of each month and chart the trend. The visual feedback loop of watching your number grow is the most powerful motivator on the path to seven figures.

At a 30% savings rate, you will get there in approximately 22 years. At 50%, approximately 17 years. There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the US based on total net worth (assets minus liabilities, including home equity), according to the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances. If you exclude primary residence equity and count only investable assets, the number is approximately 14-15 million households. Either way, the US has more millionaires than any other country.

Approximately 17% of US households have a net worth of $1 million or more. That is roughly 1 in 6 households. If measuring only investable assets (excluding home equity), approximately 11-12% of households qualify. The percentage has been growing steadily — it was about 7% in 2000.

Overwhelmingly self-made. Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (10,000+ surveyed) found that 79% received zero inheritance. Only 3% received an inheritance over $1 million. The primary wealth-building mechanism was consistent investing in employer-sponsored retirement plans (401(k)s and IRAs) over 25-30 years. The myth that most wealthy people inherited their money is not supported by the data.

The average American millionaire reaches $1 million in net worth at age 49, according to multiple studies. However, this average includes people who started investing late. FI community members who begin saving 30-50% of their income in their 20s frequently reach millionaire status by their late 30s or early 40s — a decade ahead of the average.

Yes, but it requires discipline and time. Saving 20% of a $50,000 salary ($10,000/year or $833/month) invested at 7% real returns would reach $1 million in approximately 30 years. Increasing savings to 30% ($15,000/year) compresses the timeline to approximately 25 years. It is slower than higher earners, but it is mathematically achievable — and many millionaires built their wealth on middle-class incomes.

$1 million supports $40,000/year in spending at a 4% safe withdrawal rate. Add average Social Security benefits ($22,884/year for a retired worker in 2024), and that is about $62,884/year. Whether this is "enough" depends on your location and lifestyle. In a moderate cost-of-living area, it is comfortable. In San Francisco or New York City, it is tight. The FI community recommends calculating YOUR specific number based on YOUR spending — $1 million is a milestone, not necessarily a finish line.

There are 22 million millionaire households in the US — and the data consistently shows they got there through consistent saving and investing, not inheritance, luck, or extraordinary income. The average millionaire earned a solid but not exceptional income, lived below their means, invested in diversified funds for 25-30 years, and avoided consumer debt. If that description sounds familiar, it should — it is the exact blueprint the FI community follows. You do not need to be born wealthy or earn a six-figure salary to join the millionaire club. You need a savings rate above 20%, a low-cost index fund, and enough time for compound growth to do its work. The 22 million millionaires before you have proven it works.

#9405. How to write your retirement message or announcement at work

Retirement is the end of an era. And while it’s thrilling to finally have time to do all the things you’ve been meaning to do, leaving behind your coworkers, especially if you’re close, can feel bittersweet.

To bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time. But what do you say? How can you possibly sum up years of collaboration, chaos, and connection in just a few sentences?

Nobody wants the stress of staring at a blinking cursor, so here are a few tips for announcing your retirement and writing a thoughtful goodbye message to the people you’ve worked with. By adapting them to fit your specific role and personality, you can acknowledge the relationships that mattered, offer an authentic goodbye, and leave with intention. Happy retirement!

You might think that your retirement messages need to be a perfect balance of professional, funny, and sweet, but what’s most important is that you sound like yourself.

To ensure that your note is polished and professional, keep these tips in mind.

Most people don’t want to read a long email, no matter who it’s from. A few honest lines work perfectly.

“The time has come. After 12 years of wearing the same pants four out of five days of the week and drinking lukewarm coffee from the break room, I’m retiring. I’ve truly loved working with you and appreciate every wild and wonderful day we shared.”

“Before I officially retire, I wanted to say thank you for this beautiful ride. You’ve all been unforgettable and lovely to me. You’re the reason this job didn’t feel like work.”

“After 18 years, I’ve officially graduated to more peaceful days filled with puzzles and midday naps. Logging off now, grateful for every moment. I will miss you all!”

💙 As you head into retirement, reflect on all the good times you had at work. Gratitude for the Day with Chibs Okereke can help you tap into those positive feelings.

Gratitude makes goodbye messages feel a little warmer. Think about the people or experiences that left a mark, like the coworker who knew your coffee order by heart or the one who always lent you their umbrella when it was raining. (If you need some more guidance, here are eight tips to cultivate an attitude of gratitude.)

“I want to thank my chosen family who made this workplace so special. Your support, humor, and occasional emergency snack stashes got me through some tough days and made the good ones even better.”

“Thanks to everyone who made me feel welcome, challenged, and appreciated. You’re the reason I stayed as long as I did. Well, that, and Barbara’s famous cheesecake. I’ll miss you all (almost as much as I’ll miss all the cake).”

“A heartfelt thank you to my team — you made me better every day. I’m so lucky I got to be a player on this incredible squad. Rooting for all of you always. Can’t wait to hear about all that you accomplish.”

A little story can go a long way. In addition to reminding people of the good times, it can make your message feel more original. You don’t have to write a novel, and it doesn’t need to be profound — just aim for real.

“I’ll never forget the power outage of 2019 when we all played trashcan basketball while waiting for the lights to come back on. We made the best out of a tough situation, and that speaks to the type of amazing people you are. Please stay in touch!”

“Monday mornings just won’t be the same without our doughnut runs. Thanks for the memories, team.”

Let people know all that you’ve learned while working and what you’ll carry forward. Not only will this help fill up your cup, but it can also remind people what they’ve learned while working with you. (Here are 20 questions to help with any potential writer’s block.)

“This job taught me a lot about leadership, teamwork, and that I don’t need to talk louder while I’m on zoom. (Still working on that one…) But most of all, it reminded me how amazing it is to work with such loyal, thoughtful people. I’ll never forget it. Thank you.”

“Beyond the spreadsheets and deadlines, I’m leaving with lifelong friendships, a few more well-earned wrinkles, and countless memories.”

“This place taught me how to lead, how to listen, and how to troubleshoot a broken coffee machine under pressure.”

Some words of encouragement, a simple goodbye, or even a little glimpse of what’s next for you can be a sweet way to sign off.

“I’m off to spend more time traveling, playing with my grandkids, and mastering the art of sourdough once and for all. Wishing you all continued success — and a little less time in meetings.”

“Wishing you all smooth launches, strong coffee, and at least one good laugh a day. Keep crushing it.”

“I’ll be around — probably in sweatpants, gardening gloves, or both. Don’t be a stranger.”

💙 Consider listening to Endings with Tamara Levitt if you’re having a hard time saying goodbye to your work and the people you’ve met there.

It can be tempting to sneak out, but saying farewell to your coworkers is a kind thing to do — and it can help you too. Here’s why:

1. It gives you closure on your terms: Retirement can be a tough transition. One day, you have 50 emails and several meetings, and the next, your inbox is at zero, and you have nothing but time on your hands. Writing a goodbye message can help you mark the transition.

2. It opens the door for real connection: When you write a farewell message, you’re inviting people to respond. What better way to leave than by clearly seeing the impact you had on your coworkers?

3. It lets you shape your own legacy: Your goodbye message can be a tiny chance to shape how people remember you. Go out on a positive note — literally.

💙 Writing to a coworker who’s retiring? These retirement wishes can help you find the right words.

An announcement and a goodbye note do different jobs. The announcement shares your news and your last day. The thank-yous and memories from the tips above can follow it.

Manager first: Tell your manager before anyone else, so the news doesn’t reach them through a group email.

Timing: If you can, send the announcement a few weeks before your last day so people have time to say goodbye.

Subject line: Use a clear one, like “My retirement news.”

Opening lines: Lead with the news, then name who will cover your work.

Long tenure: If you’ve been at the company for decades, add a sentence or two about your time there, and keep the news first.

Here’s an example for someone who’s been at a company for a long time: “I started here 30 years ago, and my last day will be March 31. Over the next few weeks, I’ll be handing off my projects to Marcus and wrapping up my open work. If you’d like to catch up before I go, please grab time on my calendar. I’d love to see as many of you as I can.”

You don’t have to send a retirement message, but it can be one of the simplest ways to wrap up this chapter with a bit of closure and grace. After all, you’ve spent a lot of time with these people over the years.

Writing a short, thoughtful message can help you leave on a kind note. You might also be surprised at how meaningful even a few lines can feel, both for you and the people reading them.

There’s no one right way to send a retirement message. If you want to keep it casual, you could say something like, “After 15 years, I’m off to find out if daytime TV lives up to the hype. Thanks for the talks, laughs, and memories.”

A more heartfelt message you could send is: “It’s been a true honor to work alongside so many talented people. I’m leaving with deep gratitude for my time here — and for all of you.”

If humor’s more your vibe, you could say: “Today’s my last day. Thanks for the memories — and for being so nice about the fact that I was always muted on Zoom. You’d think after a few years, I’d learn my lesson, but I digress. You’re the best, and I’ll miss you.”

Your tone depends on your personality and your workplace culture. If you’re in a very professional environment, a more formal message is the best way to go, but if your usual emails include memes and inside jokes, it’s okay to joke around.

In general, the best retirement messages usually sound like the person writing them, so trust your voice and just be yourself. You’ve earned the right to say goodbye on your terms.

There isn’t a standard checklist, but here are a few good touchpoints that can help you find your flow:

Share a bit about what you’ve learned on the job.

Consider sprinkling in your future plans.

Yes. Email is often preferred in the workplace, as it allows you to reach everyone and provides people with an opportunity to reply.

Whether you send it to your whole team or just a few close coworkers, an email is a low-stress, high-impact way to say farewell. Just remember to hit “send” before IT cuts your access!

If you’re retiring, your thank-you message to colleagues works best when it says who you’re thanking and what they did for you. You can add it to your retirement announcement or send it as a separate note.

For the whole team, a few lines are enough: “Thank you all for the patience and the laughs. Working with this team has been the best part of my job.” For one person, name something specific: “Dana, thank you for answering my questions in my first year. I couldn’t have learned this job without you.” If coworkers gave you a send-off or a gift, a short note afterward can say thanks again.

#9404. 17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

Laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together

Josh (New Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”

Laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature

Angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a plan, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students quickly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is important to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals

Jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom)

Joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

David (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful

Susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”

Related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a BIG SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome

Donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity

#9402. How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

And at times in my life, I have been a real runner. I ran a marathon in my 20s and a couple of half-marathons in my 30s. In my 40s, I mostly just made spectacular plans every January and September: I’d find exciting destination races to train for, join a gym and a yoga studio, sign up for running challenges, and pick out elaborate training plans. I’d run three or four days a week for a week or two, and then nada. Zippo. Zero runs per week.

Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

So I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious plans produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

Success is motivating. Doing what you said you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a big part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate plans but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a plan so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

I hate the idea of abandoning my big plans. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

Expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

At some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this new behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

It’s hard to abandon our grand plans and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

Join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

#9401. Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, said:

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9400. Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

Marble marvels: the Liebieghaus team deduced that the sculpted group on the Parthenon’s east pediment featured the two Dioscuri horsemen seen on this Roman sarcophagus lid at the Galleria Borghese Photo: © Galleria Borghese

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

But now, Brinkmann says his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on new findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”

The east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann says, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

The rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail)

Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main

The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

“He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”

Although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann says. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”

They discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674)

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3

None of these reliefs showed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

The team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann says. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann says. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann says. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

It is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann says. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027

#9399. 5 best essential oils for anxiety (and how to use them)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

It’s mid-afternoon, and your to-do list keeps growing. You reach for the small bottle of lavender essential oil on your desk, hold it a few inches from your nose, and breathe in slowly. Your shoulders drop, and the list feels a little more manageable.

Essential oils are everywhere these days, from store shelves to social media feeds, and you’ve probably heard the promise that lavender can ease stress and anxious feelings. When worries pile up, a quick ritual like that can sound appealing. Still, it’s worth asking how much these oils can really do for anxiety.

Ahead, we’ll cover what the research says about essential oils for anxiety, and how to try them at home.

Essential oils are concentrated plant extracts. Makers draw the aromatic compounds out of flowers, leaves, bark, peel, or resin, usually by steaming or pressing the plant. What’s left is a potent oil that carries the plant’s scent.

Aromatherapy is the practice of using these scents to ease stress and lift your mood. When you inhale a scent, the molecules reach receptors high in your nose that connect to the limbic system, a part of the brain involved in emotion and memory. That link is one reason a smell can bring back a memory or shift your mood before you've had time to think.

Essential oils may take the edge off anxiety, but think of them as a comfort alongside established treatments, not a substitute for them.

A 2023 systematic review pooled dozens of randomized trials and found that essential oils lowered both in-the-moment and overall anxiety levels compared with unscented oil or usual care.

Early results look promising, though they come with a few caveats. Most of those trials were small, and many measured anxiety in medical settings, such as the nervous stretch before surgery, rather than the everyday worry most people deal with. Results also varied widely from study to study.

If your anxiety is intense and disruptive to your daily life, talk with a doctor or therapist.

💙 Not sure if it’s stress or anxiety? Here’s how to tell the difference.

Some essential oils have far more anxiety research behind them than others. These five come up most often in studies and in aromatherapy practice. Your scent preference matters here, so you might respond to one oil and not another. Start with the one that appeals to you most.

Lavender smells floral and herbal, with a clean, slightly woody edge. It’s the most studied oil for anxiety by a wide margin, and its main compound, linalool, may help calm the nervous system.

A lavender oil capsule called Silexan was tested in a 10-week trial of adults with generalized anxiety disorder, where it reduced anxiety more than a placebo capsule. Since Silexan is swallowed rather than inhaled, the results say little about lavender aromatherapy.

If you’re new to essential oils, lavender is a gentle place to start: its scent is familiar to most people, and it’s widely available.

Neroli comes from the blossom of the bitter orange tree, Citrus aurantium. Its scent is sweet and floral, with only a hint of citrus.

In the 2023 meta-analysis, bitter orange oil ranked at or near the top of the oils tested for both in-the-moment and overall anxiety. It didn’t clearly outperform lavender, though, and far fewer trials back it up.

Unlike bergamot and other citrus peel oils, neroli hasn’t shown sun-sensitivity problems. Even so, as with any oil, dilute it and patch-test first (see the safety notes below).

Rose, often sold as Damask rose oil, smells sweet and floral. In the same 2023 review, it was the second most studied oil after lavender. Rose oil was linked to lower in-the-moment anxiety, mostly in trials of people facing medical procedures.

Pure rose oil is one of the pricier options, since it takes a mountain of petals to make a small bottle. Fortunately, a little goes a long way, and a few drops in a diffuser can scent a room.

Chamomile oil smells soft, warm, and a little like apple, which suits an evening wind-down.

In a randomized trial, older adults who inhaled chamomile oil for a month had lower anxiety scores than those who received a placebo.

In a separate hospital trial, people with heart conditions who breathed in chamomile oil for two nights had lower anxiety than those given an unscented oil.

Bergamot is the citrus that gives Earl Grey tea its signature scent: fresh and zesty, with a softer, sweeter edge.

In one randomized controlled trial, people in treatment for substance use were given bergamot aromatherapy. They reported lower anxiety than those who received standard care alone.

Bergamot and other citrus peel oils can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you apply them to your skin, keep that area out of direct sun for a day or so.

There are several ways to use essential oils, so try a few and see what works for you. Here are the four main methods:

Diffuse: Add a few drops of oil and water to an electric diffuser to scent a room. This gentle method suits a bedroom or home office.

Inhale: Hold the bottle a few inches from your nose and take a slow breath. You can also put a drop on a tissue and smell that instead.

Apply to skin: Always dilute essential oil before it touches your skin. Mix a few drops into a carrier oil, such as jojoba or coconut, then rub a little on your wrists, temples, or the back of your neck. If you’d rather skip the mixing, pre-diluted rollers are a convenient option.

Add to a bath or shower: For a bath, mix a few drops into a carrier oil or unscented bath base, then pour it into warm water. For a shower, put a few drops on the shower floor, away from the running water, and let the steam carry the scent. Oil can make the floors slippery, so step in carefully.

💙 At bedtime, turn on your diffuser and listen to The Lavender Valley, a Sleep Story on Calm that follows a stroll toward a heavenly scent.

Buy from a reputable brand, since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t check essential oils for purity or strength.

Patch-test first: dab diluted oil on a small area of skin and wait 24 hours to check for redness or itching.

Avoid direct sun on skin where you’ve applied citrus peel oils, like bergamot, because they can make skin more sensitive to sunlight.

Don’t swallow essential oils without guidance from a qualified healthcare professional.

Keep essential oils away from children and pets, since some oils are toxic to animals.

Check with your doctor if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or managing a health condition, as some oils aren't recommended.

Aromatherapy can be one part of a wider wellness routine. Use oils alongside other habits that may help with anxiety, like gentle movement, breathing exercises, time outside, and meditation. For instance, smelling lavender before a guided meditation can help you settle in.

💙 To round out your routine, explore these six natural ways to ease anxiety.

💙 Pair your aromatherapy with Calming Anxiety, a five-minute breathing meditation on Calm.

Lavender is the most studied oil for anxiety, which makes it a popular first pick. That said, scent preference matters, so the oil you enjoy most may suit you best. Neroli, rose, chamomile, and bergamot are also common choices, with some research to support them.

Essential oils may help you feel less anxious, and studies have found a modest calming effect, especially in stressful moments. However, the research is limited, especially for everyday anxiety.

If your anxiety feels frequent or intense, or if you’re having panic attacks, reach out to a doctor or therapist for support. Oils can be one small part of your routine, but they can’t replace medication or therapy.

You can put diluted essential oil on pulse points, like your wrists, temples, the back of your neck, or behind your ears, where body warmth helps release the scent. Mix the oil into a carrier oil first, and avoid putting citrus oils on skin that will be in direct sun.

At home, you can diffuse a few drops of essential oil, inhale from the bottle, apply diluted oil to your skin, or add an oil blend to a bath. Pick the method that fits your space and routine.

Frankincense is a popular choice for relaxation, but research on its effects on people is still limited. Most of the evidence comes from animal studies on one of its compounds, incensole acetate, which reduced anxious behavior in mice. If you enjoy its warm, woody scent, it may still be worth trying.

Aromatherapy uses essential oils on purpose, while smelling something nice can mean anything pleasant, from fresh-baked bread to your favorite candle. With aromatherapy, you can pick a scent and diffuse it or breathe it in from the bottle. Both can lift your mood, but aromatherapy makes smelling the scent a habit.

Essential oils can irritate sensitive skin, so it helps to dilute them in a carrier oil and patch test first. If you have a skin condition like eczema, ask your doctor before trying aromatherapy, or skip skin contact and use a diffuser instead.

International Essential Oils Day is on July 11 every year. It’s a day to celebrate essential oils and the ways people use them for well-being. If you’ve been curious about aromatherapy, it’s a good time to try it.

You don’t need much to take part. Choose an essential oil that appeals to you, such as lavender or rose, and add a few drops to a diffuser. Then take in the scent with a few slow breaths or a short meditation. If you already use oils, you could try a new scent or build a wind-down habit around a favorite.
