#9397. Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time. In the 1980s, under Yugoslavia’s “soft” one-party government, Padejski and her friends read Western literature, watched Hollywood movies, and listened to the BBC.

“We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski says.

That changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics. Civil war broke out, and a virulent strain of nationalism took hold in Serbia, the Yugoslavian state where Padejski lived. Firebrand leader Slobodan Milošević ascended to power and began meddling in elections, targeting opposition leaders, and igniting ethnic cleansing campaigns.

“He captured the entire society and his party,” Padejski remembers. “Very soon I found myself on the streets protesting.” Padejski’s activism against repressive Serbian regimes would continue until 2011, when she and her husband, investigative journalist Djordje Padejski, left the country after people threatened to kill them.

The Padejskis arrived in the U.S. with hard-won knowledge of how to outlast repression over the long haul. In recent years, they’ve tapped back into that knowledge and shared it with those around them as they witness here in America the illegal destruction of government agencies, election tampering, and warrantless arrests of citizens and non-citizens. This isn’t just true in the United States—around the world, democracy is declining.

How can we go on defying rising authoritarianism when no clear endpoint is in sight? Psychology and motivation research complement the experience of people like the Padejskis by addressing how to conserve energy and sustain commitment to your ideals in challenging conditions.

“The goal of the authoritarian regime is to desensitize us to extremes, to things we should never agree with or consider normal,” says Djurdja Padejski, now a language and culture researcher (and doctoral candidate) at Arizona State University.

Surviving repression depends on rejecting this presumed “normality” and refusing to let your inner state mirror extremes imposed from above. To that end, here are seven research-backed ways to subsist under indefinite duress.

Life under repression feels exhausting due to the colossal scale of so much of what is happening: attacks on the free press, denial of life-saving aid to millions overseas, ongoing ICE killings on the streets and in detention facilities. Reading about such developments understandably triggers feelings of overwhelm. Research finds that these feelings can drive people to shut down their emotions, dampening their motivation to help in concrete ways.

Djurdja Padejski has come to recognize that to avoid that trap, she has to face her human limits squarely without drowning in self-recrimination. As a young adult under Milošević’s rule, she learned early that worrying about what she couldn’t do was a waste of time and energy.

“It is very important not to get stuck in that moment, not to be clutching your pearls,” she says. “We have to be strategic to preserve our resources.”

Admitting your own lack of control over the big picture can be a necessary prelude to taking the actions still available to you, Padejski says. “We have to see [the situation] for what it is, so we can focus our efforts on keeping our minds, our bodies, and our communities as healthy as possible under the circumstances.”

Once you’ve gotten clear about what is within your power to control, you can get granular by carrying out regular acts of “micro-resistance.” These acts of defiance do not require you to upend your daily rhythms or put your life on the line. They can be as simple as attending a march, supporting a neighbor at an immigration court visit, or wearing a shirt with a resistance slogan.

Micro-resistance acts—such as creating protest art and continuing to study even when their department was banned from the university—helped sustain both Padejskis through years of repression, reminding them of the power they had despite limits imposed from on high.

“These micro-level actions add up,” Djordje Padejski writes. “Even small acts of defiance can maintain your sense of agency.”

Self-described “small-time” lawyer Daniel Suitor excels at this kind of micro-resistance. During ICE raids in his hometown of Minneapolis, he channeled his overwhelm by signing up for a course on how to file legal paperwork to free unjustly detained Twin Cities residents.

After Suitor filed his first case, he found out surprisingly quickly that he’d won and that the man he was representing would be freed. That proof-of-concept case spurred him to file another legal petition, then several more in quick succession. And he wasn’t alone in his commitment: To date, Minnesota lawyers have filed more than 1,000 cases challenging unjust detentions.

Acts of micro-resistance can also help prime us for future courageous action. When people perform smaller acts of selflessness and service, large-scale heroism becomes easier to contemplate, explains Medical College of Wisconsin heroism researcher Zeno Franco. Concrete practice can make you more adept at translating abstract ideals into action.

“You need to understand beyond theory,” Djurdja Padejski says. “We actually, as humans, can’t imagine how concepts work in [the] real world unless we experience them hands-on.”

For the Padejskis, one of the most stifling aspects of life under Serbian autocracy was not knowing when the repression would lift, if at all.

Periods of confinement, literal or figurative, are more bearable when a clear endpoint is in sight, and indefinite periods of repression feel uniquely oppressive. A third or more of incarcerated people with open-ended sentences suffer from depression. Others feel rooted to the present moment, severed from any potential future.

“I simply try to live in the here and now and not to plan,” one prisoner told the University of Bern researcher Irene Marti, who studies open-ended confinement. “Because I don’t have any future or only one that is very far away.”

When the endpoint of repression is uncertain, or when a challenging situation has no clear natural limit, creating your own intermediate endpoints can help you stay committed to your goals and values.

In a recent goal-setting study, when people broke an annual community service goal into granular sub-goals (say, four hours of service a week, or eight every two weeks), they volunteered more hours in the long run than people without intermediate goals.

In the same way, committed resisters can pledge to put in a set number of hours each week, or carry out a set number of clearly defined actions. According to self-determination theory, choosing and pursuing your own accessible goals boosts your well-being and motivation—internal changes that persist even when the larger crisis remains ongoing.

As governments around the world curtail freedom of speech and movement, it’s hard not to feel the noose tightening. One way to create more existential breathing room is to consider how this moment fits into the longer arc of history.

This helps you subsist in the present by reminding you of parallel past moments (whether decades or centuries ago), how they came to a head, and what ultimately resolved them. Research finds that when people take a long-term perspective, reflecting on recent stressful events as though they happened far in the past, they report less emotional distress in the moment.

Djurdja Padejski found solace in doing this during Milošević’s reign. “I survived that period mostly by reading the columns in the newspapers,” she says. One column in particular, by Serbian anthropologist Ivan Čolović, examined the regime’s activities from a broader historical and social perspective.

“He was offering a vocabulary and a theoretical apparatus to help us deal with the horrors of civil war. The news about it was the most severely censored, the propaganda was relentless, and all of it was new for many of us who were children when the fallout of our world began,” Padejski says. “That’s how I survived with my sanity intact, because it helped me to recognize what is happening to society.”

Among the most potent present-day energy drains is the social media industrial complex that feeds on people’s rage and frustration, serving up extreme viewpoints that deepen entrenched social divides as they rack up likes and views.

“Social media and internet platforms—they’re amplifying what is also a typical quality of authoritarian regimes. They’re all about grandiosity,” says Djurdja Padejski, who studies the linguistic mechanisms of propaganda. “Algorithms grab people’s attention by intensifying the language and the visuals and the overall framing.” That’s a big reason why frequent social media use saps your cognitive resources and motivation, making it harder to subsist under repression.

Plugging this energy drain requires not just limiting your time online, but redirecting more of that time to the in-person, small-group exchange to which humans are uniquely suited.

When you engage with people face to face, it’s much harder to reduce them to a stereotype or particular viewpoint. And by getting to know them in all their messiness, contradiction, and complexity, you bond with them in ways that lighten the mental and practical load for everyone involved.

“To resist this reduction of our existence to, ‘What are you for or against?’ means embracing creativity, art, friends, communal projects, protests, walks,” Padejski says. “These 10 years of resistance [in Serbia]—I honestly remember it as a series of walks. Sometimes that meant running away together from Milošević‘s militias or the official police, or from water cannons, or rubber bullets. But what is left is our conversations on ideas, on creations.”

Though exchanges like these may not further resistance directly, they form the edifice that sustains it. Within bonded human-scale communities, members have a clear sense of not just their own energetic capacity, but that of others in the group. That means they can pinch-hit for one another: When someone needs help, they can fill in on the spot—or, like relay racers, take up the baton when someone needs to withdraw. This shared flexibility and responsiveness help all group members to stay committed for the long haul.

For the Padejskis, subsisting under Serbian repression meant homing in on the values that were most important to them, and upholding those values even if it meant sacrificing convenience or comfort. When Djordje Padejski needed a lifesaving drug, a relative told him he could work his connections to obtain the medicine, but only if Padejski joined the Serbian dictator’s political party. Padejski refused, knowing that doing so put his health at risk.

The couple have continued that tradition in the U.S., though in somewhat less life-altering ways. After Elon Musk unleashed an apparent Nazi salute at a Trump post-inauguration event, the Padejskis gave up their Tesla. “I drive a Subaru now,” Djurdja Padejski says. “I really don’t like it compared to Tesla, but I don’t regret it.”

Some people write off such moral stands as more symbolic than substantive. But symbol, it turns out, shapes substance: What you stand for predicts and influences what you’ll do down the road, for good or ill. When people have a clear, consistent moral identity, studies find, they’re more likely to take real-world action aligned with that identity.

On the other hand, when you’re willing to cave on something that seems minor, like supporting a complicit business, “you are detached from your inner beliefs, from what you know is real and good and safe,” Djurdja Padejski says. “Once you’re there, you are ready to compromise a lot of values that you think you are really one with.”

One unexpected thing the Padejskis learned, under Milošević and afterward, was the importance of not swinging into action every time a devastating piece of news hit. Overcommitment amounted to self-sabotage, sapping energy and resources they’d need later on.

Military commanders have long known the importance of “keeping their powder dry,” Zeno Franco points out, holding back so they can act at the moment of maximum impact. In the same way, the best long-distance runners often hang back throughout a course to conserve energy, then uncork a burst of speed in the race’s final minutes.

Djurdja Padejski followed this principle to great effect under Milošević. She bided her time leading up to the critical elections of 2000, then worked tirelessly as an election volunteer to monitor for irregularities and make sure no one was falsifying results. All the while, ruling party members with guns lurked in the background.

“This guy started opening his gun and checking the bullets, and we didn’t cave. We just ignored him,” Padejski says. “We knew we were risking our lives, but we really believed it’s now or never.” Serbia’s democratic opposition party ultimately won that election, causing Milošević’s downfall.

Padejski hopes democratic activists around the world will take a similar approach as crucial elections near. Under repressive conditions, keeping your powder dry “is not an instruction to put off action as long as possible, but rather the wisdom to know that being prepared to act at just the right moment may require careful guarding of resources and energy,” Franco says. “Biding your time is not the same as surrender.”

Elizabeth Svoboda is the author of What Makes a Hero?: The Surprising Science of Selflessness. Her upcoming book, The Art of Pacing, is about setting a sustainable pace in a speed-obsessed world.

#9396. The Positive Personality Trait Linked To Having A Crush Outside Your Relationship

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a new attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone new.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, showed a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also showed a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

#9395. Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create new jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her new book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

With loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “company” for the lonely?

The harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

For example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

While it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that says ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

Turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

Unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

Interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

“For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

Turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

Though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, says Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

“Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

Of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” says Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”

Turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

“If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our plan, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”

Turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

For example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

“Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”

A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”

Whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with new iterations, there is increasing agreement on one issue: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

“The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”

Still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”

To this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

“We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

While her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

“When we see these choices with new clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is important for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

#9394. South London Gallery director Margot Heller to leave role after 25 years

Margot Heller photographed inside the exhibition Monika Sosnowska: Weight of Matter at the South London Gallery

Margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years. Over this time the institution’s physical footprint has more than tripled and visitor numbers increased tenfold, according to a gallery statement.

Heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser. She will retain a connection with the gallery, curating the Dutch artist’s Mark Manders’s first solo exhibition at a London institution, opening at SLG on 23 September 2027.

“After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career,” Heller said in a statement.

“From the day I took up the role, I saw an opportunity to build an institution that could be internationally acclaimed for its contemporary art programme, and deeply embedded in its local community. I have stayed true to that vision ever since.”

Serge Ramin, the chair of the gallery’s trustees, described Heller as “a visionary curator and cultural leader”, adding: “She leaves a museum that is artistically ambitious, rooted in its community and physically transformed.”

Heller’s tenure encompassed two major building projects with 6a architects: the conversion of a neighbouring house and construction of an education studio in 2010, followed by the opening of the former Peckham Road Fire Station in 2018.

The fire station was donated in 2014 by the artist Raqib Shaw, whose identity was initially withheld. Its conversion cost £4m. Heller told The Art Newspaper in 2018 that the gallery had not been actively seeking to expand when the building was offered.

A garden designed by Gabriel Orozco opened in 2016, while Art Block, the gallery’s free space for children and young people on the neighbouring Sceaux Gardens estate, opened at its current site in 2017.

The artist and SLG trustee Alvaro Barrington said: “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own.”

He added: “Her commissioning of the Orozco Garden should be considered one of the most important architectural interventions in the UK.”

Exhibitions Heller has worked on during her tenure include solo presentations by Steve McQueen, Rashid Johnson, Oscar Murillo, Michael Armitage and Christina Quarles. The gallery was a joint winner of Art Fund’s Museum of the Year award in 2020.

Before joining the SLG, Heller worked at Southampton City Art Gallery, becoming its director, and as director of exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery. She was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2014.

The gallery became an independent charity in 2003, having previously been managed by Southwark Council.

Joy Gregory, an artist and SLG trustee, said of Heller in a statement: “As a local resident and artist, I am enormously grateful for the extraordinary legacy she leaves behind and excited to see what she does next.”

South London Gallery in Peckham (aka Little Lagos) will show work of 13 artists including Yinka Shonibare, bringing to light the shared cultures of the two places

#9393. 12 happy Thanksgiving greetings and messages to share

Thanksgiving is a time to reflect on everything—and everyone—you’re thankful for, but expressing those feelings, especially to the people who matter most, isn’t always easy.

You might struggle to find the right words to tell your family or friends just how much you care, or maybe you’re not sure what’s appropriate to say to your colleagues or business partner. You’re bound to brighten someone’s day no matter what you say, but it can be helpful to have a few suggestions on hand.

This guide will help you craft meaningful Thanksgiving greetings for every important person in your life. From warm and sentimental messages to professional and appreciative ones, we can help you find the perfect words to share gratitude and reflect on your connections.

You may associate Thanksgiving with turkey and all the trimmings — but it’s really time to celebrate the people you love. Whether it’s your family, lifelong friends, or the colleagues you see every day, Thanksgiving is a perfect excuse to tell them how much you care.

A heartfelt message doesn’t have to be complicated. A few sincere words can go a long way! Whether you’re writing a card, sending a text, or sharing your thoughts in person, taking the time to say something meaningful shows you care.

Here’s how you can share thoughtful greetings and make everyone in your life feel truly special this holiday season.

For many people, Thanksgiving is a time to gather with family, making it the perfect time to let them know how much they mean to you. Family often gives us our strongest foundation — offering love, support, and shared traditions that make life richer. A quick text or call can go a long way in showing your gratitude, and you might consider saying something like:

1. “Wishing you a Thanksgiving filled with love, laughter, and all our favorite traditions. I’m so thankful for the memories we’ve made together.”

2. “This Thanksgiving, I feel so lucky to have such a wonderful family. Thank you for being my rock through all the ups and downs.”

3. “Happy Thanksgiving! I’m grateful every day that you’re my family.”

Include a shared memory: Mention something specific that connects you to the recipient. For example, “I’ll never forget last year’s Thanksgiving dinner when we all laughed until we cried. Here’s to making more memories like that!”

Focus on their unique qualities: Highlight what you admire about them. You might say, “Your kindness and generosity inspire me every day, and I’m so thankful to have you in my life.”

Express anticipation for the future: If you’re celebrating together, add a line about how much you’re looking forward to it, such as, “I can’t wait to see you and enjoy Mom’s famous pumpkin pie together!”

Friends are the family we choose, and Thanksgiving is the perfect opportunity to let them know how much they mean to you. Whether it’s the friend who always knows how to make you laugh, the one who listens when you need to talk, or the group that feels like home, these connections deserve to be celebrated.

4. “Happy Thanksgiving! Your friendship means the world to me. Thank you for bringing so much joy into my life.”

5. “Here’s to great friends, good food, and gratitude. I’m so thankful for the laughs and support you’ve shared with me this year.”

6. “Wishing you a Thanksgiving as amazing as you are. Thank you for always being there and making life so much better.”

Acknowledge their impact on your life: Mention specific ways they’ve helped or supported you. For example, “I’ll always be grateful for the time you helped me through a rough patch. Your kindness made all the difference.”

Celebrate shared moments: Bring up a memory that captures the essence of your friendship. For example, “I’m so thankful for our road trip this year — it was one of the best vacations of my life!”

Show excitement for future plans: If you have plans to celebrate together or see each other soon, include that in your message. For example, “I can’t wait to watch the Thanksgiving parade with you this year — it’s my favorite tradition!”

💙 In her Gratitude Masterclass, Tamara Levitt teaches you to unlock the transformative power of this life-changing practice.

Your colleagues play an important role in your daily life. Whether it’s collaborating on projects, sharing laughs during lunch breaks, or supporting each other through challenges, the relationships you build at work can make your life much more rewarding.

Expressing appreciation to colleagues doesn’t have to be complicated — and if done well, it can foster a more collaborative work environment. (In the meantime, here are 13 tips for effective communication at work.)

7. “Happy Thanksgiving! I’m so grateful to work alongside you. Your dedication and positivity make a difference every day.”

8. “Wishing you and your loved ones a joyful and peaceful Thanksgiving. I’m thankful for your hard work and the kindness you bring to the workplace.”

9. “I truly appreciate everything you do and the impact you have on our team. Have a great (and relaxing) Thanksgiving!”

Acknowledge specific contributions: Highlight something they’ve done that stood out to you. For example, “Your leadership on our last project really inspired me. I’m grateful to have you as a colleague.”

Reflect on shared experiences: If you’ve had a particularly positive moment working together, bring it up. You could say, “I’ll always remember how we pulled together for the big presentation last month — it was such a team effort!”

Use a friendly, conversational tone: While professionalism is important, don’t be afraid to let your personality show. For example, “Hope you get to kick back and relax this Thanksgiving — you’ve earned it after all the hard work this year!” And if you work with a distributed team, try putting something cheerful in a group email or on Slack or Teams to build camaraderie.

You’re probably thankful for your career, and if you provide a service of any kind, your clients are a big part of that. A thoughtful Thanksgiving message can show your appreciation, set the tone for a continued relationship, and acknowledge the role they play in your success. Plus, when you take the time to say “thank you,” you’re building goodwill, deepening trust, and showing that they matter beyond their business.

10. “Happy Thanksgiving! We are truly grateful for your trust and partnership. Working with you has been a pleasure, and we wish you a season filled with happiness and success.”

11. “As we reflect on the past year, we’re reminded how fortunate we are to work with incredible clients like you. Thank you for your support, and we wish you a happy Thanksgiving!”

12. “Wishing you a wonderful Thanksgiving! We deeply appreciate your business and look forward to continuing our partnership in the year ahead.”

Mention specific successes or collaborations: For example, “Your trust during our product launch earlier this year meant so much to us. Thank you for helping us achieve that milestone!”

Express excitement about future opportunities: Share your enthusiasm for continuing the relationship. You could say, “We’re excited to see what we can achieve together in the coming year!”

Incorporate a small token of appreciation: If appropriate, consider pairing your message with a thoughtful gift, such as a branded item, a box of treats, or a donation made in their name to a charitable cause.

💙 Learn the secret to stronger connections with our Relationship with Others series.

Instead of “Happy Thanksgiving,” you could use phrases like “Wishing you a Thanksgiving filled with love, laughter, and cherished memories” or “I hope you have a great holiday, and a few slices of pie.” “Happy Thanksgiving” is still a classic, but a more personal phrase may help your message stand out.

For someone you’re especially thankful for, you can go a step further by expressing how much they mean to you, maybe including some specific details or examples. The key is to speak from the heart.

Personalizing your message starts with thinking about your relationship with the person. For family, consider mentioning shared traditions or memories that make Thanksgiving special for you. For example, you could write, “I’ll always remember how we all used to watch football together before gathering around grandma’s table.” Acknowledging shared experiences shows how much you value the bond you have with them.

For friends, focus on the qualities that make your friendship unique. A message like, “Your kindness and sense of humor have made this year so much better — thank you for being such a wonderful friend” can brighten their day.

When it comes to colleagues, a professional yet warm approach works best. Mention how much you value their hard work, teamwork, or support, like, “Your dedication and positivity inspire me every day. I’m so grateful to have you as a colleague.”

When crafting Thanksgiving messages for clients or business partners, it’s important to strike the right balance between professional and personal. The tone should reflect gratitude for their trust and collaboration while maintaining a polished and respectful vibe. For example, a message like, “We’re deeply thankful for your continued support and trust in us. Wishing you and your loved ones a wonderful Thanksgiving,” conveys both professionalism and warmth.

If you’ve worked closely on a specific project or achieved significant milestones together, mentioning those can add a thoughtful touch. For instance, “This year, your partnership helped us achieve some truly amazing things, and we’re so grateful for your contributions. Here’s to more success in the coming year!” This approach not only expresses thanks but also highlights the value of your ongoing relationship.

One simple way to incorporate gratitude practices into your Thanksgiving celebration is to go around the table and ask everyone to share what they’re grateful for.

You can also write thank you notes to people who have made an impact on your year. These don’t have to be lengthy — even a few sentences can make someone feel appreciated. If you’re celebrating with family or friends, consider surprising them with a small note expressing why you’re thankful for them.

You might also consider giving back to your community, which can be incredibly fulfilling. Volunteering at a local shelter, donating to a food bank, or helping a neighbor in need are all ways to show gratitude through action. These practices not only enhance your Thanksgiving but also leave a positive impact on those around you. To cultivate a stronger sense of gratitude, try these eight tips.

Thanksgiving cards are a thoughtful way to share your gratitude, and adding a creative touch makes them even more special. One idea is to include a photo — this could be a family picture, a snapshot of your team at work, or even an image of a past Thanksgiving celebration. Photos instantly make a card feel more personal and nostalgic.

You could also include a short, heartfelt message or even a simple poem about gratitude and the season. If you enjoy crafting, consider making a DIY card with autumnal designs like leaves, pumpkins, or warm color palettes. Adding small details like handwritten notes or a ribbon tie are nice too.

For digital cards, don’t be afraid to use design tools or templates to create something unique. A thoughtful e-card can still feel personal if you take the time to craft a meaningful message. What matters most is the care and effort you put into creating and sending it.

Thanksgiving greetings are about more than just words — they’re a way to connect, show gratitude, and spread warmth during this time of year. By tailoring your messages and including a personal touch, you’ll make each greeting that much more meaningful.

A good Thanksgiving greeting card message names the person and says one thing you’re thankful for about them. It can be a single line or a longer note, depending on how well you know them.

For a close friend or family member, you might write, “Thank you for showing up for me this year. I’m grateful for you today and every day.” For a neighbor or a teacher, something like, “Thank you for being so kind to our family this year. Wishing you a warm and relaxing holiday,” works well.

A card gives you more room than a text does, so you can add a memory or a detail only the two of you would know. If you’re stuck, write the way you’d talk to them. A sign-off like “With gratitude” or “Thinking of you” can finish it off.

#9390. 10 types of breathing exercises and techniques to try

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

We all have those days. Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

Breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

In this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

Breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

There are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

You may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

Helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

When life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

As one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

How to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

This type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

How to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and quickly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

How to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

This technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

Alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

How to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

This technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory issues. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

The lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood quickly.

How to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise

Also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

How to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

Use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

How to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

Breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

How to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

Practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

Many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

When anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

If you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

If you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

Surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

In fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to quickly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.

#9389. UK government places export ban on Mughal calligraphy works valued at £900,000

The Mughal-era calligraphy albums were sold by Islamic and Indian art specialist dealer AeR Gallery in London

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

“By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” says a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

The calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

According to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735)

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport

Meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, says in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”

The painting from 1662 depicts the Llannerch Park country estate in northeast Wales, and is valued at £550,000

#9388. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In a genre built around sweetness and ease, one “cozy” video game did something far greater: It put me back together after I lost Mary.

Mary was not only my then-boyfriend’s mother, but she also became an important maternal figure when my own family life felt unstable. I accompanied her on weekly grocery store runs that included stops at Marshall’s and Dollar Tree, where I’d watch her study the prices of everything from spices to bath products. When she saw me marveling at her meticulousness, she would share wise tidbits about how she looked for deals.

Our trips often ended with a late-afternoon stop at a Vietnamese restaurant, where she treated me to a warm bowl of beef pho. She’d share what she was excited to make for dinner; I was, of course, welcome to join. In these seemingly mundane afternoons, I felt cared for without the rush of obligations. Mary stopped time for me.

Last November, Mary left behind a world of loved ones after living with cancer for 14 months. From her living room to emergency stays in the hospital, I spent almost every single day of her fight by her side. Yet in my loneliest hours, I agonize over whether I fully cherished our last months together. Did I hug her enough, and did I tell her enough how much she means to me? These questions haunted me in the months afterward.

Funny enough, it wasn’t religion that rescued me; it was Pokémon Pokopia. On the surface, it is a new social simulation game featuring the iconic Japanese creatures who first took the world by storm in 1996. I first heard of its arrival on social media through gamers who raved that it was going to be the best game of the year. I grew up on Pokémon titles, so I recognized it as a distraction from my personal reckoning with abandonment.

But what began as a spur-of-the-moment decision to try what 4 million other gamers were playing turned into a transformative journey exploring what I want my life to mean when it feels as if I have been left behind.

Pokopia falls in the “cozy” game genre, beloved for its warm colors, gentle atmospheres, and easy missions. Released in March, Pokopia stars Ditto, an amorphous purple blob Pokémon that uses its transformative abilities to imitate its human trainer and rebuild a curious post-apocalyptic world devoid of human beings and Pokémon. Ditto first awakens in a cave, and as the story unfolds, the creature looks out at a once-grassy environment of parched earth and litter. It meets the first Pokémon, the hydrophilic Squirtle that teaches Ditto how to spray water across the thirsty soil to bring it back to life; it is also the only other semblance of a survivor in this barren land.

From here the story gains momentum: As Ditto, your mission is to get the environment back to habitable levels and bring back Pokémon creatures that are presumably hiding. Gradually, the unfinished railroad tracks and cracked concrete steps of a staircase stop looking like signs of a catastrophe but rather fixable problems.

I wasn’t alone in trying to find meaning after a loss or trauma. Scholars have explored a variety of constructs around the meaning of life. Psychologists Login S. George and Crystal L. Park articulate a three-part framework in their 2010 article, grounded in comprehension, purpose, and mattering, as a basis for assessing our judgments and feelings as we find meaning after loss.

At first, meaning seemed absent. I sat glued to my Nintendo Switch for three hours on my first day of play. I came up for air only when my console told me that I was low on battery. Yet I did not feel depleted; I had finished restoring the first environment in the Pokopia world to verdant levels with lush berry trees and waterfalls.

As I built new habitats, I met new Pokémon. A Charmander emerged among tall grass. A Cubone spawned from a gravesite surrounded by wildflowers. Every new Pokémon that resurfaced charmed me with their excitement to be back home, scampering across the grass to greet other familiar faces. In my mind, I thanked these creatures for turning to me. Without Ditto’s help—my help—a world of Pokemon creatures ceases to exist, fated to disappear alongside humanity.

After a Pokémon spawns in its revived habitat, it awakens with some surprise. “Huh?” “What?” Some of them startle and put up their defenses in front of Ditto, who then coaxes them into the reality that they are back in a safe, familiar home. Often this realization gives them relief. “Wow, you did all of this? Thank you!”

Some of the Pokémon seem more wistful. They hold on to items or articles of clothing that their trainer used to wear, like the oversized Tangrowth (a large Pokémon with thick, shaggy vines that cover its entire body) that wears a pair of glasses much too small for him that gamers can infer are its trainer’s. Other creatures comment on Ditto’s human-like appearance (“You look like your human!”). These private conversations between Pokémon affirm that Ditto, who is also piecing together where its own trainer has gone, is doing something meaningful.

In 2023, game scholars Karam Eum and Young Yim Doh explored how bereaved adults shaped a meaning-making experience by playing video games with narratives that focus on loss and grief. Subjects spent a week playing two different video games and kept a diary where they shared specific game scenes that were particularly meaningful. While the games did evoke sad memories, participants also recalled positive memories in their pre- and post-loss lives, be it a funny conversation or a serendipitous moment shared with close ones who are still alive.

In the real world, the player behind the console, I, too, wonder where my beloved human has gone. I see Mary in the pink rose bouquets at grocery stores, and I smell her in the fragrant bone broth that wafts from the next-door apartment unit. In some of these most visceral disruptions, I feel my loss painfully.

But even in these heaviest of days, I surrender to the ordinary surprises that come up: a call from an old neighbor asking if I can help make meals for a family in need, or a stray cat mewing at my window to open the building’s front gate. I am startled out of a detached state, and I am moved to help, the way I got to help Mary.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

I associate Mary now with the colorful berry trees in Pokopia. When I come across one that needs tending, I remember how easy it is to water it with my Squirtle-like powers. When I clear a path from blocks of beach sand to make way for a new house for my aquatic Pokémon, I think of Mary’s selfless endeavors to nourish and comfort all of her friends and family.

Despite its sad undertones, Pokopia is full of positive quests, eager to help gamers imbue its universe with the belief that it is worth building a positive world in memory of those who shaped us. Even though our loved ones may “mysteriously” leave us behind, we recreate happiness, redefine ourselves, and choose who and what we live for, even if they do not come back.

It’s curious to me that bereavement can feel so isolating, although it is a human experience universally experienced. It helps to have a video game that reminds me of the actual truth. When I start to catch myself drifting into deeper ends of grief, I have something to divert my attention: I wonder how my Ditto is doing? I pick up my Switch 2 that sits at the foot of my bed, and I make a new home for my Pokémon the way Mary had done for me.

Lisa Kwon is an arts and culture writer based in Los Angeles, CA. She has contributed to The Guardian, Teen Vogue, Vulture, Eater, Prism Reports, Cultured Magazine, National Geographic, and many more.

In three years, I lost five loved ones, my dog, my childhood home, and my sense of invincibility. What I gained was a deeper capacity for gratitude.

Couples who embrace their own “microculture”—pet names, inside jokes, and rituals—may be happier and more satisfied with their relationship.

According to an analysis of 99 studies, mental well-being leads to a longer life.

Social anthropologist and urban designer Louise Vogel Kielgast shares how thoughtful public spaces can make room for more awe and human connection in everyday life.

#9387. The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

#9384. What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.

A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”

I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.

I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim, or contact campus or local police departments.

This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?

Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.

Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.

The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.

Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence—even when this belief is wrong—inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.

Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed—in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.

Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.

This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.

Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program—focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors—report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later.

These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior.

At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.

But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team.”

Another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. Bystander intervention programs emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence.

Students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.

It’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only with college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up.

Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling—and learning specific strategies for intervening—can make a real difference.
