#9374. How to reduce screen time and improve your digital well-being

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report. You wince at the number, then swipe it away with the same thumb you were scrolling with.

Screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite shows. By evening, you can feel worn out even if the day wasn’t particularly busy.

Conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them. A few small tweaks to your daily routine are a good place to start. Below, you’ll find some realistic ways to cut back, plus a look at why it can feel so hard to put your phone down.

There's no set amount of time that counts as too much. What matters more is how your screen use affects you. Signs worth noticing include strained eyes, restless sleep, reaching for your phone out of habit, and feeling worse after scrolling. If any of these sound familiar, the tips below may help.

💙 Not sure if this sounds like you? Check out these five signs you might be online too much.

If “one more video” keeps turning into one more hour, you’re in good company. Many apps are designed to keep you scrolling, so you’ll need more than willpower to cut back. Start with one or two tips that feel doable right now. You can come back to the rest later.

Bright colors can make apps harder to put down, and notification badges and thumbnails are built to draw you in. Switching your screen to black and white takes away some of that appeal, which can make scrolling feel less rewarding.

Try: Search “grayscale” or “color filters” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under Accessibility or Well-Being.

Grayscale may look odd for a day or two. Some people keep it on all day, and others only turn it on in the evening to wind down. You can turn it off whenever you need to, like when you’re using maps or looking at photos.

💙 Listen to the Build Healthier Phone Habits series with Dr. Aditi Nerurkar on Calm.

Time can slip by while you scroll. Set a daily limit on your one or two most-used apps, and your phone will nudge you when you reach it.

Try: Search “app limits” or “app timers” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under screen time.

Start with a limit slightly below how much you use those apps now, then lower it gradually. Smaller steps are often more sustainable than cutting back all at once.

Notifications like news alerts, app promos, social likes, and game reminders mostly add noise. Keep the ones you rely on, such as texts, calls, and reminders, and turn off the rest.

Try: Search “notifications” in your device settings, then toggle off the alerts you don’t need, starting with the apps that send the most.

Constant check-ins can keep you glued to your screens all day. Pick a few set times to go through your messages, emails, and feeds.

Try: Limit your check-ins to lunchtime and after work, and keep your personal devices out of reach in between.

Before you open your phone, take one slow breath and ask yourself why you’re reaching for it. If the answer is just habit, that brief pause may be enough to snap you out of autopilot.

Try: Breathe in for four counts and out for six, then see if you still want to unlock your phone.

💙 Discover 10 types of breathing exercises you can try anytime, anywhere.

When you feel the urge to pick up your phone, try turning to an offline activity instead. Keep an activity you enjoy within reach, like a book on the couch or a sketchpad on the table.

💙 Want to work on the habit before the urge hits? Explore Tame Your Scrolling Habit with Rose Nisker on Calm.

Choose one or two spots to keep screen-free, such as the dinner table or your bedroom. A clear boundary often works better than a vague promise to use screens less. These zones also give you room to be more present, like during a family meal or your evening wind-down.

Try: Place your phone in a dedicated spot, like a basket by the door. If you share a home, invite everyone to join.

💙 Not ready to go phone-free at night? Tune in to Sleeping with Your Phone with Dr. Matthew Walker on Calm.

Pick a cutoff time for all your screens, such as 30 minutes before bed, and stick to it as best you can. Late-night screen use can keep your mind active and make it harder to fall asleep.

If you usually watch a TV show before bed, choose one episode and turn off autoplay.

Try: Schedule a nightly reminder for your cutoff. Swap your screen time for a calming activity, like journaling or a short meditation.

💙 Press play on the Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

A few common app features can keep you hooked:

Infinite scroll: New posts keep loading, so you never reach a natural stopping point.

Autoplay: The next video or episode starts on its own, which keeps you watching unless you stop it.

Unpredictable notifications: Each message or like feels like a small reward, and not knowing when the next one will pop up keeps you checking.

Your emotions play a part too. A screen can be a quick escape when you’re stressed or putting something off. It can bring relief in the moment, even if you feel more drained afterward.

💙 If your screen time has been weighing on your mood, read our guide on what to do if technology is impacting your mental health.

If you want to cut back on screen time without giving up after a few days, start small. Choose one change, like keeping your phone off the dinner table, and give yourself time to adjust before you make another tweak to your routine. If you slip back into old habits, you can always start again the next day.

To set screen time limits that stick, build them into your routine so you don’t have to rely on willpower in the moment. You could use an app timer or set aside a screen-free time each day, like the first half hour after you wake up.

There isn’t a daily screen time limit that works for every adult. If you’d like to use screens less, a good starting point is a limit slightly below your current daily average, and you can lower that limit gradually as you get used to it.

How you spend your screen time matters just as much. An hour on a video call with a friend often leaves you feeling better than an hour of doomscrolling.

You can reduce your screen time at night by setting a cutoff time before bed and charging your phone across the room. Swap your late-night scroll for a book or a short meditation to help you relax before sleep.

To help your family reduce screen time together, make it a shared plan. You could agree on screen-free times, such as during meals or the first hour after school or work. Try leading by example, rather than telling your kids or partner what to do.

No, you don’t have to quit screens completely to feel better. Technology connects you to the people and things you care about. You can cut back on the screen use that leaves you feeling worse, like aimless scrolling, and keep what you value.

#9373. Sotheby’s makes last-minute deal to sell $180m Van Gogh painting following dispute

The Blaquier family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) in 1975

Sotheby’s today announced that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in New York.

The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

The Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”

The provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

Last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he says took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”

The Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

Looted by the Nazis, after the war it was returned to the Rothschild family

“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”, which has been hidden away for over 60 years, is being sold by Sotheby's for the Blaquier-Arrieta family of Argentina

The Nazi-era claim, resolved just hours before the Sotheby’s New York sale, appeared to have little impact on the final price

Back-to-back New York auctions made a combined $777.8m, with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas proving bright spots in an evening marked by uneven bidding

#9372. Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

In a new study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves showed less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

The new research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, said Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

“Collaborative relationships are important for our well-being, health, and survival,” said Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November issue of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

Scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who showed signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

Then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

Chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov said.

Researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

The thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov said.

Jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, said previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

“We expect more of our friends,” said Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”

The paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

“We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov said. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”

This article was originally published on Berkeley News. Read the original article.

Jason Pohl is a science writer in UC Berkeley's Office of Communications & Public Affairs.

#9371. How cognitive behavioral therapy works to treat OCD

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next. For some people, it’s checking the locks again and again, even when they know the door is shut. For others, it’s washing their hands until they feel clean, counting steps or objects, arranging things until they feel just right, or getting stuck on an unwanted thought.

What unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop. But the relief doesn’t last and you end up back at the anxious thought, triggering the process again. For people living with OCD, this cycle can be exhausting.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most studied ways to break the OCD cycle, and one type in particular, called exposure and response prevention (ERP), has the strongest research support of any talk therapy for OCD. Here’s a look at what CBT for OCD involves, how ERP works, and what a session can feel like.

CBT is a structured, evidence-based form of talk therapy. It looks at how your thoughts, feelings, and actions feed each other, and it focuses on the present rather than digging through your past. Most versions help you notice unhelpful thoughts and respond to them in new ways.

CBT for OCD works a little differently. With something like anxiety or low mood, a therapist might help you question a worried thought and look for more balanced evidence. With OCD, that technique can backfire. Trying to argue with an intrusive thought, or prove it wrong, can become a mental compulsion, which keeps the cycle going.

So OCD-focused CBT spends less time debating the content of your thoughts and more time changing how you respond to them. The main tool for that is ERP, a type of CBT that focuses on behavior.

If you've ever been told to "just stop worrying," you may know that advice doesn’t work for OCD. The cycle doesn’t respond to willpower alone.

You get an intrusive thought or fear you don’t want (the obsession)

To get relief, you do something to make the feeling go away (the compulsion), like checking, washing, asking for reassurance, or going over events in your mind

You feel better, but only for a short while

Each compulsion can teach your brain that the thought was a true threat and that the ritual kept you safe. So the thought tends to return.

Say you’re leaving for work. A thought pops up: What if I left the stove on? Your anxiety spikes, so you go back and check. The stove is off, and you feel relief. But on your way to the car, the doubt returns, along with the urge to check again.

That's why OCD can feel impossible to overcome. The very thing that calms you in the moment is what feeds the cycle.

ERP involves gradually facing the things that trigger your fears, while holding off on the compulsion. It can sound intimidating, but it’s planned and step by step, and you and your therapist agree on each move together. Here’s what it tends to look like.

A lot of questions up front: Early sessions are mostly about getting clear on what's happening. Expect to talk through your intrusive thoughts, the compulsions they trigger, and the situations you avoid.

Building a fear ladder: Your triggers get ranked from mild to most distressing, and you start near the bottom. You won't be asked to face your worst fear on day one.

Facing triggers on purpose: You'll meet a fear instead of dodging it, whether that's touching a doorknob, writing down a feared word, or sitting with an uncertain thought.

Not doing the compulsion: Expect to resist the response you'd normally reach for, even something subtle like seeking reassurance.

Sitting with the discomfort: At first the fear climbs, which can feel like proof it won't stop. Over time, many people find the fear eases, and they learn they can cope with it.

Homework between sessions: Practice between sessions is a big part of progress, so expect to take exposures home and work on them in your daily life.

ERP with a trained therapist is the core of OCD treatment, and nothing below replaces it. But the stretches between sessions can be long, and a few grounding habits may make them easier to deal with.

Mindfulness and meditation can help you practice noticing a thought, letting it pass, and not acting on it or trying to prove it wrong. That fits well with ERP, where you also learn to let urges be present without giving in. A few minutes a day can be a gentle place to start.

One caution: if you catch yourself meditating to “cancel out” a bad thought, that’s the compulsion sneaking back in. The aim is to let thoughts come and go, not to get rid of them.

💙 Practice noticing a thought and letting it pass with Chibs Okereke’s short Working With Thoughts meditation.

When you’re struggling with anxiety or a racing heart, slow breathing can help your body settle. Box breathing is one option, since the even count gives your mind something simple to hold onto.

Use it for everyday stress, like after a tough commute or before bed. During an exposure, or when you’re trying to make a thought go away, it can work against ERP, because the point is to practice facing the discomfort. Ask your therapist when it’s okay to use it alongside your ERP practice.

💙 For a tense, jittery day, Panic SOS with Kirat Randhawa uses sight, sound, and touch to help your body settle.

Poor sleep and OCD symptoms often go hand in hand. Research links poor sleep to more intrusive thoughts and harder-to-manage symptoms. Rest may also make it easier to do your ERP practice.

A steady routine can help. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time each day, and dim the lights and put screens away 30 minutes or so before bed. A warm shower, gentle stretching, or a sleep meditation can help you unwind, and limiting caffeine later in the day may make it easier to fall asleep.

Bedtime can be a hard time for those of us with OCD, as quiet moments can leave room for intrusive thoughts, checking, or reassurance-seeking. If rituals are keeping you up, mention it to your therapist.

💙 Give your mind permission to power down with this Wind Down (for Sleep) session on Calm.

Putting your obsessions, compulsions, and triggers on paper may help you and your therapist spot patterns you’d otherwise miss. Many people find it easiest to jot down a few quick notes each time the loop shows up: what set it off, what thought or fear came up, what you did in response, and how you felt afterward. Over time, you may notice that certain places, times of day, or moods make the cycle more likely.

While you’re mapping the loop, try not to judge yourself or over-analyze your entries.

💙 If you’re struggling to get started, journaling prompts can help.

A walk around the block, a stretch, or a few minutes of dancing in your kitchen can help ease stress and give your body a reset. Pick something that feels possible even on a hard day, and tie it to something you already do, like a few minutes of movement while your coffee brews or after you hang up a call. Doing it at about the same time each day can also help it stick.

One thing to watch for: if movement starts to feel like a ritual, like needing to take a certain number of steps or repeat a routine until it feels “just right,” mention it to your therapist.

💙 Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Walking series turns a short stroll into a chance to notice what’s around you.

OCD can be isolating. Talking with a friend or family member you trust can remind you that you’re more than your symptoms. If a loved one wants to help, ask your therapist how. Well-meaning support, like answering the same reassurance question again and again, can accidentally keep the cycle going, and a therapist can guide you both.

A peer support group can also help. Reputable OCD organizations run groups where you can meet people doing the same work.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most effective treatments for OCD, especially a type called exposure and response prevention (ERP). Research shows it can reduce symptoms for many people.

CBT helps by targeting the anxiety cycle that keeps OCD going. Depending on how severe symptoms are, it's used on its own or alongside medication.

Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the best-studied therapy for OCD, but it isn’t the only option. Other approaches include cognitive therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and inference-based CBT (I-CBT). Cognitive therapy helps you examine the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel threatening. ACT focuses on making room for uncomfortable thoughts rather than fighting them. I-CBT targets the reasoning that makes an obsession feel believable. Medication, usually a type of antidepressant called an SSRI, is a separate treatment that can lower the intensity of symptoms. It’s often combined with therapy. A clinician can help you weigh which mix fits your situation.

ERP, or exposure and response prevention, is a type of CBT where you gradually face your triggers while resisting the urge to do a compulsion. It's a first-line treatment for OCD.

Each time you sit with a fear and resist the ritual, your brain gets evidence that the feared outcome doesn't arrive and that the distress is survivable. That learning is what loosens OCD's grip. A therapist structures the exposures so they stay challenging without tipping into overwhelming.

The main difference is what each approach targets. Regular CBT often focuses on changing unhelpful thoughts, such as questioning a worry and replacing it with a more balanced one. CBT for OCD focuses on the compulsion.

That’s because, with OCD, the compulsion is what keeps the cycle going. Each time you do the ritual, or try to prove the fear wrong, your brain learns that the thought was a real threat and the ritual kept you safe. In ERP, you face the trigger and hold off on the compulsion. Over time, your brain learns that the feared outcome doesn’t happen and that you can cope with the anxiety without the ritual. Some therapists also work on the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel so threatening, but ERP is the main tool.

Cognitive distortions are unhelpful thinking patterns, and in OCD they often show up as beliefs that make ordinary doubts feel dangerous. Common examples include:

Feeling responsible for preventing harm, even when it’s unlikely

Overestimating how likely something bad is to happen

Thought-action fusion, or believing a thought is as bad as an action

Struggling with not knowing for sure (intolerance of uncertainty)

Assuming a thought must matter because you had it

These patterns are common in OCD, and they can fuel the urge to do compulsions. Therapy can help you spot them and loosen their grip.

💙 Find out more about cognitive distortions and how to reframe negative thoughts.

Many people see meaningful improvement from ERP within about 12–20 sessions, which is often three to four months with weekly visits (intensive programs can be faster). Some notice shifts with fewer sessions, especially with regular practice in between.

Timelines vary with symptom severity, how often you practice, and whether medication is part of the plan. OCD treatment is usually designed to be relatively short-term and skills-based, not open-ended.

You can do some ERP on your own, and self-help books and apps exist for it, but working with a trained therapist is strongly recommended, especially for moderate to severe OCD.

Self-directed ERP can be tricky to get right. It can be easy to accidentally turn an exposure into a subtle compulsion, or to skip the exposures that matter most. A therapist keeps the plan honest and adjusts it as you go. If therapy isn't available right now, guided self-help from a reputable OCD organization is a safer starting point than going it fully alone.

Mindfulness can support OCD treatment, but it isn't a standalone fix. Research on mindfulness for OCD is promising but mixed, and ERP remains the first-line treatment.

On its own, mindfulness won't switch off intrusive thoughts, and expecting it to can backfire. Its real value is helping you relate to those thoughts differently, which is why it pairs with therapy rather than replacing it. A clinician can point you toward using it in a way that helps.

💙 If you’d like to try it, these tips for practicing mindfulness meditation are a gentle place to start.

#9370. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark new insights. This is particularly important because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

#9369. This Vitamin Deficiency May Double Heart Disease Risk

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results showed that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, said:

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very important to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This said, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially important, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

#9368. Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, Cambridge, Massachusetts Photo: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons

The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, said during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”

Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she said. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

#9367. 25 unique experience gift ideas for everyone on your list

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Maybe you’ve had the experience where you’ve opened a gift that didn’t quite land… Another candle, another kitchen gadget, another book you probably won’t read.

When life can feel increasingly materialistic, receiving the gift of an experience can feel like an extra special treat. A coffee date, a class you could take together, or a simple invitation to step away from your routine for a few hours. Gifting experiences is becoming more common as people increasingly value things to do rather than things to have. Experiences create memories, prolonged joy, and ways to connect and bond with your loved ones.

Let’s explore why this trend is becoming a thoughtful option for many, and how to choose the right option for the people in your life.

Gifting an experience means offering someone the chance to do or enjoy something, rather than giving them a physical item. It could be a short outing, a shared class, a small adventure, or even a moment of relaxation. The focus is on creating a meaningful interaction or memory.

At its core, an experience gift acknowledges who someone is and what matters to them — comfort, curiosity, connection, or rest. It’s a way of saying, I see what brings you joy or ease, and building a shared experience around that. This can feel especially supportive for people whose lives are busy or emotionally stretched.

Because these gifts are flexible, they work across relationships and budgets. They can be shared or solo, active or restful, planned or open-ended. They offer a moment that feels nourishing and special for someone you care about.

💙 If relaxation is what they need, a Calm gift card gives them access to sleep support, meditation, and stress tools.

While research on experience gifting is still growing, studies highlight how shared time and supportive interactions can strengthen relationships and help people feel more connected.

And for the giver, choosing an experience can relieve some of the pressure to pick the “perfect” item. Plus, you get to be a bit more creative since experiences can be catered to the person in question more accurately than a new sweater or scented bath salts.

These gifts also tend to linger in memory. A walk through a new neighborhood, a class where you learned something together, or an afternoon spent doing something familiar but intentional can shape how people feel long after the moment ends. The emotional takeaway is often stronger than anything wrapped.

Choosing an experience gift doesn’t need to feel complicated. A few gentle questions can help you find something that feels both thoughtful and doable:

Will this support connection in a way that feels natural?

These considerations keep the focus on care rather than wow-factor. The most memorable experience gifts are often the ones that feel easy to say yes to.

Related read: What is the receiving gifts love language? Plus, 10 examples

Experience gifts don’t have to be big, expensive, or Instagram-ready. The most meaningful ones usually feel simple, personal, and easy to follow through on. Below are ideas for different people in your life, with concrete examples and small tweaks to make each one feel low-pressure yet purposeful.

1. Slow morning together: Gift a “no-alarm morning” where you plan nothing except being together. This could look like making breakfast at home, wandering to a café, or staying in pajamas with a movie. You can write it as a simple coupon: “One slow morning: no chores, no plans, just us.” This works well for tired partners who crave rest more than busy plans.

2. A shared learning experience: Choose a class or workshop that feels fun. Cooking, pottery, a dance class, a cocktail-making session, or even a virtual class from home. The goal is to play, not create a new skill. Pick a time that fits your usual schedule, and make it clear there’s no pressure to be good at it. You’re just trying it out.

3. A “memory lane” date: Revisit places that matter to your relationship: where you met, a favorite early date spot, or a park you love. You can build a simple route and add tiny prompts, like sharing a favorite memory at each stop. This turns a regular outing into something personal without costing much.

4. At-home retreat night: Create a mini retreat without leaving the house. That might mean takeout, candles, phones off for a few hours, and a shared activity like a puzzle, show, or playlist swap. You can include options on a card so they can choose: a massage, a movie, a board game, or just some quiet time together.

5. Surprise “care afternoon”: Block off a few hours for them where you take on a task they’ve been dreading—organizing a small space, handling an errand, or taking something off their mental load—and then follow it with something relaxing, like a walk or coffee. The experience is both practical support and quality time.

6. Future adventure fund: If money is tight or schedules are messy, create a “future adventure” envelope. Add a small amount of money, a short list of possible outings (day trip, concert, special restaurant), and a promise to choose an option together when life settles a bit. The gift is the intention and shared planning, not just the event itself.

💙 Explore 5 Steps to Stronger Relationships with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Related read: How to build emotional connection in relationships

1. Family game or movie night: Plan a night with a few easy games or a movie everyone can enjoy. Add snacks, cozy blankets, and a pause on chores for a few hours. You can give the night a “ticket” and let family members vote on the game or film. Keep it simple so no one has to host a perfect event.

2. Seasonal outing: Choose something tied to the time of year: apple picking, a beach afternoon, a holiday light walk, or a picnic in the park. The key is to keep expectations reasonable. Pick something close by, flexible with the weather, and not too long. Add a warm drink stop or simple treat to make it feel special.

3. Family photo walk: Go for a walk through a neighborhood, park, or favorite spot and take casual photos of each other and everyday moments. This isn’t about staged portraits. It’s about capturing small, real pieces of your life together. Later, you can print a few favorites as a follow-up surprise.

4. Shared creative project: Start something you can all contribute to: a family recipe book, a small garden, a scrapbook, or a shared playlist for car rides. The “gift” is the first session to begin the project, plus a plan to keep it going at a relaxed pace.

5. Story or memory night: For older family members, gift a relaxed evening where you ask about their stories — childhood, early jobs, favorite memories. You can record audio or write things down if they’re comfortable. This can feel especially meaningful for grandparents or relatives who don’t often get to share their history.

6. Chore-free experience swap: Offer to trade time: you handle childcare, yard work, or a big errand so another family member can enjoy their own experience like a class, a nap, a solo walk, or quiet time at a café. The experience you’re gifting is space and freedom, which many busy adults crave more than objects.

💙 Family life feels overwhelming? Check out the Ease Parenting Stress series with Jeff Warren on the Calm app.

Related read: Here's why you should establish family values (and how to do it)

1. Friendship field trip: Pick a spot you’ve both wanted to visit, maybe a new café, nearby town, market, bookstore, or trail. Make it simple: transportation, one planned stop, and room to wander. You can name it something fun on the card, like “Field Trip Day: You + Me + Snacks.”

2. Theme night at home: Instead of going out, bring the theme to your living room. Taco night, cozy soup night, DIY spa night, or favorite childhood snacks night. The gift is that you plan the details so your friend just shows up and relaxes. This works well for introverts or friends on a budget.

3. Shared creative time: Gift a “creative hang” where you both bring whatever you want to work on like, drawing, writing, knitting, music, or even organizing photos. Add music, snacks, and low-pressure conversation. For friends who feel guilty about not making time for hobbies, this can feel like a gentle permission slip.

4. Local class or workshop together: Check out low-stakes options like pottery, candle making, painting, or a casual fitness class. Pick something that doesn’t require special gear or skills and frame it as an experiment, not a performance: “We’ll probably be bad at this, and that’s half the fun.”

5. Walk-and-talk ritual: Offer a series of scheduled or flexible walk-and-talks. Maybe once a month, every other week, or whenever you both can manage. The experience is regular emotional check-ins built into movement and fresh air. If walking isn’t accessible, this can be a sit-and-sip ritual at a park or café.

6. Volunteer outing: Choose a cause you both care about and sign up for a shift together. Serving food, helping at an event, or supporting a community project. It can create a shared sense of meaning and connection beyond your usual routine, and it doesn’t need to be a big time commitment.

💙 Learn more about Meaningful Practice for Meaningful Friendship on the Calm app.

Related read: How to be a better friend: 7 tips to improve your relationships

1. One-on-one “date” with you: Plan a simple outing centered around their interests like ice cream, a playground, a comic shop, the library, or a favorite café. The important part is your undivided attention — no multitasking, no rushing. You can make a small “VIP pass” with their name and the activity.

2. Activity day pass: Gift a trip to a kid-friendly place: zoo, aquarium, children’s museum, climbing gym, trampoline park, or mini golf. To keep expectations realistic, include what’s covered (entry, one snack) and how long you’ll stay. That clarity helps avoid meltdowns.

4. Backyard or park adventure: Create a small “explorer kit” experience. Maybe that’s a printed map, a simple scavenger hunt, or nature bingo. Then take them to a nearby park or backyard to complete it together. The kit can be as simple as a folded paper with things to look for: birds, leaves, colors, shapes.

5. Choose-your-own-activity coupon book: Instead of one big outing, make a few small coupons they can redeem over time: “Stay up 30 minutes late,” “Pick tonight’s dinner,” “Board game together,” “Extra story at bedtime.” This spreads the experience out and gives them a sense of choice.

6. Screen-time with purpose: If screens are part of your life (for most families, they are), turn it into an intentional experience. A planned movie night with popcorn and cozy blankets, or a co-op video game session where you play alongside them. The shift is from “background screen” to “shared screen time.”

7. Skill-building mini lesson: Offer to teach them something they’ve shown interest in, like basic cooking, drawing, sewing, photography, or music. Keep it short and fun — 30 to 60 minutes with lots of breaks. The experience is meant to help them feel capable and supported, not pushed to master something.

Related read: 61 fun and simple mindfulness activities for kids to enjoy

Good experience gifts feel easy to enjoy and don’t add pressure. Simple outings like a coffee date, museum visit, or nature walk work well, as do classes or small day trips.

If you’re unsure, think about what the person already loves—quiet spaces, creativity, movement, or social time—and choose something that gently supports those interests.

Budget-friendly experience gifts often center on time or support rather than cost. A homemade coupon for help with errands, a movie night at home, or a walk together can feel more meaningful than anything store-bought.

You can also offer a few options, like a baked treat, a playlist walk, or a shared hour of connection, so the gift feels personal without being expensive.

Experience gifts ease the pressure of traditional gifting and help strengthen connections. They don’t create clutter and often require less guesswork than choosing an item.

Because they create memories, they can feel more lasting and emotionally meaningful. Early research also suggests shared time and supportive interactions may help people feel more connected.

Examples include classes, tours, local events, shared meals, creative workshops, or simple nature outings. They can also be quieter moments like helping with a task or planning a cozy night in.

Even small gestures—like sharing a playlist—count. The impact comes from the feeling the experience creates, not the size of the activity.

If you’re unsure, offer a few choices rather than picking one activity. Options like a coffee outing, nature walk, or game night let the person choose what fits their energy. A flexible gift card to a café, movie theater, or class platform also works. Choice keeps the gift from feeling like an obligation.

Families often enjoy simple, low-pressure activities that include everyone. Seasonal outings, game nights, and local events work well because they’re easy to plan.

Shared projects—like cooking or gardening—or gifts of time, such as taking on chores so someone can rest, can also be meaningful. The best family gifts support connection without adding stress.

Friends tend to appreciate experiences that feel connecting and relaxed. This might be a field trip to a new café, a creative class, a cozy night in, or a shared walk.

Some friends enjoy active outings, while others prefer crafting or volunteering together. The goal is to match their energy and make time together feel restorative.

Experience gifts can feel better for some people because they avoid clutter, reduce pressure, and often feel more meaningful. They shift the focus toward presence and memory-making rather than buying things.

While not everyone prefers experiences, they offer a gentle alternative for people who value connection or feel overwhelmed by physical items.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you plan to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Company). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

The biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

The 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the important thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and company handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.
